title: The wolf of Gubbio (Little Flowers 21)
hookLine: a legend of Francis making peace between a wolf and a town

lines: A TOWN AFRAID TO GO OUT.
A SMALL MAN WALKS TOWARD IT.
cards: The town of Gubbio has stopped going outside. A wolf, huge and fierce, has been killing animals in the fields, and people too.

Anyone who leaves the walls goes armed, as if heading into battle, and plenty don't leave at all. Into this town walks a small man in a patched habit. He hears about the wolf, and says he's going out to meet it.
The people beg him not to. He makes the sign of the cross and walks out anyway, the townspeople climbing wherever they can to watch. Today, a legend from the Little Flowers.

teach.b: The wolf charges. Francis makes the sign of the cross over it and calls it by a family name: Brother Wolf. Come here, he says, and in the name of Christ, do no harm to me or to anyone.
In the story the wolf closes its mouth, slows, and lies down at his feet like a lamb. Then he talks to it straight: you've done great harm.
You've killed God's creatures, and people made in God's image, and the whole town is against you. But I want to make peace between you and them.

teach.h: THE WOLF KILLS BECAUSE IT'S HUNGRY.
teach.b: Here's the turn: Francis has noticed why the wolf kills. It's hungry. So the peace has two sides.
The wolf will harm no one, and the town will feed it for as long as it lives, so hunger never drives it to harm anyone again.

teach.h: A PAW LAID IN HIS HAND.
teach.b: Francis asks for a pledge and holds out his hand, and the wolf lays its paw in his palm. In the town square, in front of everyone, the bargain is made again, paw and all.
After that, the story says, the wolf went from door to door, the people fed it kindly, and no dog barked at it. People read the legend in more than one way.

teach.h: THE TOWN FEEDS ITS FORMER ENEMY.
teach.b: Some read a real animal and a real wonder; some, a picture of a town and its enemy, a fierce man perhaps.
Either way, Francis doesn't kill the wolf or chase it off. He gives it a brother's name, and asks what it needs.

how: The wolf of Gubbio is one of the stories told about Francis in the Little Flowers, and Catholics, especially Franciscans, retell it in sermons, art and children's books as a story of peacemaking.

games.q: what does “the wolf of gubbio” mean?
o: a wolf that guarded Francis on all his travels
a legend of a hungry wolf tamed by peace, not by force
a fable about a wolf punished for attacking a town

games.q: the wolf and the town — tap the pairs.

s: in the story, Francis drives the wolf out of Gubbio
he makes peace: the wolf harms no one, and the town feeds it.
Francis notices that the wolf kills out of hunger
so the peace has two sides: no more harm, and food for the wolf.
the pledge is made only once, outside the walls
the wolf gives its paw outside the town, then again in the square in front of everyone.

games.q: you're Francis. the wolf is lying at your feet, and the whole town hates it. what do you do?
o: tell the wolf to leave and never come back.
ask the town to feed it, if it harms no one.
let the townspeople decide its fate.
games.why: Francis makes peace with two sides: the wolf promises no harm, and the town promises to feed it for life.

practice: Bring to mind something prowling around the edges of your life, a conversation you dread, a worry about someone you love, and let it come near, the way the wolf came near, without running at it or from it.

Then ask it Francis's question: what does this fear actually want, maybe safety, an answer, to be taken seriously? If you pray, make the sign of the cross and hold it before God; if not, breathe with it at arm's length.

wordCard.voice: The wolf of Gubbio. A legend of a hungry wolf, a frightened town, and a peace where each side gave something. Today's word.

orig.note: Italian, the language of the Little Flowers: brother wolf.

carryVoice: Your line: brother wolf. The peace had two sides, and the town kept its half. Until tomorrow.
